quote: Auf wie viel Parameter kann eine vorgelegte Gl. durch Lösung einer Gl. niederer Ordnung reduciert werden?
english: To how many parameters can a given equation be reduced by solving an equation of lower order?
topic: A list of research questions: reducing the number of parameters in an equation by solving equations of lower order, literature on equation theory in Mathematische Annalen, non-associative or non-commutative composition rules, and approximate counting of solutions of Diophantine inequalities by lattice points in a pyramid.

triage.modern_statement: Take a general polynomial equation of degree n, f(x) = x^n + a1 x^(n-1) + ... + an. You are allowed rational operations, Tschirnhaus transformations and the solution of auxiliary equations of lower degree. What is the smallest number of essential parameters (coefficients) that the equation can be reduced to? In modern terms this is the resolvent degree RD(n) of the general degree-n polynomial, more generally of a finite group or branched cover (Brauer 1975; Farb–Wolfson). For small n it relates to Hilbert's Sextic conjecture (RD(6)=2), his Octic conjecture (RD(8)=4) and his 1927 paper on the degree-9 equation (RD(9)≤4).
triage.answered_by: It has not been fully answered. Hilbert published the question himself as his 13th Problem (1900), later wrote 'Über die Gleichung neunten Grades' (Math. Ann. 97, 1926/27), and stated the Sextic and Octic conjectures. Arnold and Kolmogorov (1957) solved only the continuous-function version, not this algebraic one. R. Brauer (1975) gave the modern definition of resolvent degree. Recent work: Farb and Wolfson ('Resolvent degree, Hilbert's 13th Problem and geometry', L'Enseignement Math., arXiv 1803.04063); Wolfson's upper bounds for RD(n); Sutherland; Heberle and Sutherland (arXiv 2110.08670); Reichstein; Farb, Kisin and Wolfson ('Modular functions and resolvent problems', arXiv 1912.12536). Even whether RD(n) > 1 for some n is still open.

evidence.claim: The algebraic form of Hilbert's 13th problem asks for the resolvent degree RD(n) of the general degree-n polynomial, i.e. how far the number of parameters can be reduced using algebraic functions of fewer variables.

Farb and Wolfson developed the theory of resolvent degree, introduced by Brauer, to make Hilbert's 13th Problem precise. They cite Hilbert's 'Über die Gleichung neunten Grades' and his Sextic and Octic Conjectures.
Hilbert's Sextic Conjecture is studied in modern work through level-2 hyperelliptic modular functions (Farb–Kisin–Wolfson).
New upper bounds on resolvent degree via Sylvester's obliteration algorithm, which goes back to Hilbert's 1926/27 Math. Ann. paper on the ninth-degree equation.
Quanta (2021) reports that the widespread belief that Hilbert's 13th was solved had blocked the geometric study of resolvent degree, and that Farb and Wolfson revived it.
Reichstein's survey traces the line from Hilbert's 13th problem to essential dimension and resolvent degree.

triage.why: The diary question asks how far a given equation's parameters can be reduced by solving lower-order equations. That is the reduction-of-parameters problem Hilbert later made public as the algebraic form of his 13th Problem and studied in his 1927 paper on the degree-9 equation. The page also mentions literature on equation theory in Mathematische Annalen, which fits the Klein–Hilbert resolvent tradition. Modern sources state this as the resolvent degree RD(n). It remains open, and the Farb–Wolfson program since 2018 has made it an active research area. I can't date the diary entry from what I found, so I can't say whether the note came before or after the 1900 problem list.
